notes.claim: Standard form is a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, also called scientific notation.
NIST recommends choosing prefixes so values lie between 0.1 and 1000, using only prefixes for powers of 10 that are multiples of 3.
Milli is the metric prefix for one thousandth, 10⁻³.
For i5: the BIPM's list of SI prefixes gives giga G 10⁹, mega M 10⁶, kilo k 10³, centi c 10⁻², milli m 10⁻³ and micro µ 10⁻⁶.
For i5: engineering notation differs from scientific notation only in that the exponent is always a multiple of three (Fiore).
For i5: in engineering notation prefixes replace the multiples of three, including nano n 10⁻⁹ and pico p 10⁻¹² (Fiore).
For i5: in standard form A × 10ⁿ, 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is an integer.
For i5: the ×10ˣ, EXP or EE key keeps a number in standard form together, so no brackets are needed.

sources.title: What is standard index form in maths? - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: In standard form, numbers are recorded as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten. This is also called standard index form or scientific notation

sources.title: NIST Guide to the SI, Chapter 7: Rules and Style Conventions for Expressing Values of Quantities | NIST
sources.quote: prefix symbols should be chosen in such a way that numerical values are between 0.1 and 1000, and that only prefix symbols that represent the number 10 raised to a power that is a multiple of 3 should be used.

sources.title: Milli- - Wikipedia
sources.quote: Milli (symbol m ) is a unit prefix in the metric system denoting a factor of one thousandth (10 −3 ).

sources.title: 1.3: Scientific and Engineering Notation - Engineering LibreTexts
sources.quote: The only difference between scientific notation and engineering notation is that for engineering notation the exponent is always a multiple of three.

sources.title: 1.3: Scientific and Engineering Notation - Engineering LibreTexts
sources.quote:
The prefixes are:
* E12 = Tera (T) | E9 = Giga (G) | E6 = Mega (M) | E3 = kilo (k)
* E−3 = milli (m) | E−6 = micro ((\mu)) | E−9 = nano (n) | E−12 = pico (p)

sources.title: What is standard form? - GCSE Maths Revision - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: A number in standard form is written as 𝐴 × 10(^𝑛), where 𝐴 is a number that is greater or equal to one and less than 10 (1 ≤ 𝐴 <10) and 𝑛 is an integer.

sources.title: Calculations using standard form - GCSE Maths Revision - BBC Bitesize
sources.quote: Using the ×10(^x), EXP or EE button will keep the whole number together, including the ‘times-ten-to-the-power’ part, so no brackets are needed when using that number in a calculation.
